articles.title: Apple's first touchscreen MacBook comes at a price
articles.summary: Apple's first touchscreen MacBook Pro starts at $2,899 with a PROLED XDR OLED display, but the non-touch M6 model costs $900 less at $1,999.
articles.body: Apple has finally given the MacBook Pro something many people have wanted for years: a touchscreen. The company unveiled its first touchscreen MacBook Pro on Oct. 28, introducing a new way to interact with its laptop. It also brings a stunning OLED display, a thinner design and some serious processing power. However, there's one detail that might make you think twice before reaching for your wallet. The new touchscreen MacBook Pro starts at $2,899. That's a lot of money for a laptop, even by Apple's standards. So, what exactly are you getting for that price? More importantly, will touching your MacBook's screen make enough of a difference to justify an upgrade? Let's look at what Apple has introduced and who might benefit most. Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money. Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com. 8 BIGGEST THINGS WE LEARNED FROM APPLE'S 2026 EVENT Apple finally brings touch to the MacBook Pro For years, Apple maintained that the Mac worked best with a keyboard and trackpad. Meanwhile, Windows laptop owners have enjoyed touchscreen options for a long time. Apple even experimented with touch controls through its Touch Bar, but that feature never replaced the traditional laptop experience. Now Apple has changed course. Its new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display lets you interact directly with the screen. You can scroll through websites with your finger or pinch to zoom into photos. Apple also lets you drag content between windows and interact with supported creative apps. Think about how often you instinctively touch your laptop screen, especially after spending years using an iPhone or iPad. Now that gesture will actually do something on the new MacBook Pro. Apple also redesigned the hinge to keep the display steadier when you touch it. That's a thoughtful addition because nobody wants a screen wobbling every time they tap a button. However, this remains a traditional laptop. It doesn't fold into a tablet, and it doesn't support Apple Pencil. You'll still use the keyboard and trackpad for much of your work. That may disappoint anyone hoping to replace both a MacBook and an iPad with one device. The OLED display could be the bigger story While everyone is talking about the touchscreen, Apple's new display technology might have an even greater impact on your everyday experience. The company calls it the PROLED XDR Display, and it uses tandem OLED technology. Unlike traditional laptop screens that rely on a backlight, OLED pixels produce their own light. That allows the display to show deep blacks alongside bright highlights without the same backlight glow. Apple says the new screen reaches up to 2,000 nits of peak brightness for both HDR and SDR content. It also delivers a claimed 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio and supports refresh rates up to 120Hz for smoother motion. Those numbers sound impressive, but what will you actually notice? Photos should look more vibrant, especially when you're viewing pictures taken on your iPhone. Movies can show more detail in dark scenes. If you edit videos or work with photography, the improved color accuracy could be especially useful. Apple has also added an antireflective coating to help reduce glare. An optional nano-texture finish provides additional reflection control for people who work in bright environments. For someone who spends hours looking at a laptop screen, these improvements could be more valuable than touch alone. A touchscreen MacBook Pro with serious processing power Apple isn't holding back on performance. The new touchscreen MacBook Pro comes with either an M5 Pro or M5 Max processor. Both target people who need more processing power than a basic laptop typically provides. If you're editing high-resolution video or working with large photo libraries, these chips are designed to handle that workload. Apple also offers configurations with up to 128GB of unified memory and 16TB of storage. However, those upgrades can drive the price considerably higher. The new MacBook Pro runs macOS 27 and includes Apple Intelligence alongside Apple's upgraded Siri AI. It also brings Dynamic Island to the Mac for the first time. That familiar feature from the iPhone sits near the top of the display and gives you access to live updates and useful controls. For video calls, Apple includes a 12-megapixel Center Stage camera. Meanwhile, an upgraded six-speaker system promises deeper bass. The laptop also includes Thunderbolt 5 connectivity and an HDMI port, which should appeal to people connecting external displays. 12 BIGGEST APPLE WWDC 2026 TAKEAWAYS YOU NEED TO KNOW Apple's new MacBook Pro is thinner and lighter One concern with touchscreen laptops is whether all that additional technology makes them heavier. Apple says it has managed to move in the opposite direction. The new 14-inch touchscreen MacBook Pro weighs about three pounds, roughly half a pound less than its predecessor. The 16-inch model comes in at four pounds, approximately 0.7 pounds lighter. Both models also feature slimmer designs. That should make carrying a MacBook Pro between meetings or packing one for a trip a little easier. Apple promises up to 24 hours of battery life, depending on the configuration and usage. That's an impressive claim for a machine with this much performance and such a bright display. However, we'll need independent testing to see how battery life holds up during real-world work. How much does Apple's touchscreen MacBook Pro cost? Apple has positioned its touchscreen MacBook Pro firmly in premium territory. The 14-inch model with the M5 Pro chip starts at $2,899, while the 16-inch version starts at $3,399. If you want the more powerful M5 Max processor, prices jump to $4,499 for the 14-inch model and $4,799 for the 16-inch version. And remember, those are starting prices for each configuration. Adding more memory or storage can increase the total substantially. There is another important detail. Apple introduced a separate 14-inch MacBook Pro with its newer M6 chip on Oct. 27. That model starts at $1,999, but it uses a Liquid Retina XDR Display without touch support. That means you're looking at a $900 difference between Apple's entry-level M6 MacBook Pro and its least expensive touchscreen model. Of course, the more expensive version also includes an M5 Pro processor and the upgraded OLED display. These are different performance configurations, so the additional $900 doesn't represent the cost of touch alone. For another perspective, the previous 14-inch MacBook Pro with the M5 Pro chip started at $2,499. That makes the new touchscreen version $400 more expensive than its comparable predecessor. Still, this gives you a meaningful choice. You can buy a powerful new MacBook Pro for considerably less if you don't need to interact directly with the screen. We've previously reported on how rising AI chip costs have pushed Apple prices higher. This latest introduction adds another premium option to an already expensive lineup. Will your favorite Mac apps work with touch? Apple says many existing Mac apps will respond to touch immediately because macOS can translate finger taps into mouse clicks. That should make basic interaction straightforward, even before developers fully optimize their software. However, Apple's bigger ambition involves creative applications. The company demonstrated touch controls in Final Cut Pro that let editors manipulate clips directly on the screen. Musicians can use Logic Pro to play virtual instruments with their fingers. Apple also expects third-party apps, including Adobe Lightroom and Microsoft Office applications, to take advantage of the new touch capabilities. That sounds promising. Still, a touchscreen doesn't automatically make every app easier to use. Tiny buttons and crowded menus can be frustrating when you're trying to select something precisely with a finger. Early hands-on reports suggest that touch works smoothly for common gestures. However, some smaller macOS controls can still be awkward to tap. Those are preliminary impressions rather than findings from extended testing. It will be interesting to see how quickly developers adapt their interfaces and whether people continue using touch regularly after the initial excitement wears off. Should you upgrade to Apple's touchscreen MacBook Pro? This is the question I'd ask before spending nearly $3,000. If you already own a relatively recent MacBook Pro that handles everything you throw at it, I wouldn't rush to replace it solely for touchscreen capabilities. A mouse or trackpad still gives you excellent control, especially when you're working on detailed projects. However, if you edit video professionally or spend your days working with photos, the OLED display could make a real difference. The improved portability also makes the new model appealing to people who regularly travel with demanding workloads. For everyday activities like email and web browsing, a less expensive MacBook Air or standard MacBook Pro will probably be more than enough. Before making that decision, take a look at our guide explaining how to know when it's time to replace your Mac. A computer that still performs well may have several good years left. You can also explore our best laptops for 2026 at CyberGuy.com to compare other options before committing to Apple's premium model. One more suggestion: If you're considering the touchscreen MacBook Pro, visit an Apple Store when it becomes available on Nov. 6. Spend some time using the touchscreen alongside the keyboard and trackpad. That hands-on experience could tell you more than any specification sheet. Pro tip: Don't forget to protect your new MacBook If you're spending nearly $3,000 on a new MacBook Pro, protecting that investment should be a priority. While macOS includes built-in security features, Macs can still face malicious downloads and online scams. I recommend keeping your software updated and using strong antivirus software for an additional layer of protection. Strong antivirus software can help detect malware and warn you about dangerous websites before they cause trouble. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com. Kurt's key takeaways I have to give Apple credit for finally bringing a touchscreen to the MacBook Pro. It feels like a feature that should have arrived years ago, especially when we're all so accustomed to touching the screens on our phones and tablets. I'm also impressed by what Apple is promising with its new OLED display. For people who work with visual content, that could be the most compelling reason to upgrade. But here's where I hesitate. At $2,899, Apple is asking a lot for a feature that many competing laptops have offered for years. And with the standard M6 MacBook Pro starting at $1,999, there's a pretty compelling argument for saving that extra $900. I want to see how useful touch becomes in everyday work before calling this a must-have upgrade. My advice is to try it in person before spending the money. articles.title: Does opting out of TV tracking work?
articles.summary: A new study from Northeastern University shows that while most TV operating systems respect ACR opt-outs, not all do.﻿
articles.body: The fact our TVs are gathering our information isn’t new, but what and how they’re tracking — and if we can stop it — is hard to figure out. Researchers at Northeastern University monitored 12 TVs from 10 manufacturers to test whether opting out of automatic content recognition (ACR) actually works. While opting out was effective for most TVs — including LG, Amazon Fire TV, a Sony Bravia running Google TV, and those with Vidaa OS (which can be found on TVs from Hisense, Toshiba, and smaller brands like the Supersonic used in the study) — Samsung and Roku kept sending some data. And Walmart’s Vizio TV continued on as if the opt-out hadn’t even happened. ACR systems sample the audio or video playing on a TV, convert them into digital fingerprints, and send them to a database to identify what’s being watched. TV companies use that information to make recommendations of what to watch next, provide viewing metrics, and allow for targeted ads. The researchers wanted to understand when ACR was running on each TV, whether opting out did anything, and what type of data ACR systems were capturing. Because there are many different TV operating systems, and manufacturers keep smart TVs locked down, ACR activity needs to be inferred based on where the TV sends data. --- TVs used in the study Samsung QN32Q60DAF — Tizen OS LG TV 32LR655BPUA — webOS Roku TV 32R3B5 — Roku OS TCL TV 32S350R — Roku OS Sony K-43S20M2 — Google TV OS Vizio VHD32M-0810 — Vizio OS Fire TV HD32N200A — Fire OS Supersonic SC-1520VTV — Vidaa OS Westinghouse WX24HX2800 — Xumo OS Hisense 32A4K (with no ACR) — Google TV OS TCL 32S250G (with no ACR) — Google TV OS Sony KD32W830K (with no ACR) — Google TV OS --- To answer those questions, the team developed a suite of automated experiments across all the TV operating systems. They used Northeastern’s Mon(IoT)r software and SPHERE Research Infrastructure testbeds to capture and analyze all network traffic from each TV, which let them determine when ACR tracking was active and figure out where the TVs were likely sending that data. They played content on each TV from first-party streaming services such as LG Channels and The Roku Channel; third-party streaming like Netflix and YouTube; over an HDMI cable; using the over-the-air antenna; and via screen mirroring, all to see if there was any difference in ACR traffic on different inputs. They found that several of the TVs tested didn’t seem to have any ACR activity whatsoever, including a Westinghouse Xumo TV and three TVs from Sony, Hisense, and TCL running Google TV OS. (Another Sony TV with Google TV did have ACR enabled.) Of the TVs with ACR-associated network traffic, all of them scan over-the-air transmissions, while everyone but Google and Amazon uses it on first-party streaming services (such as The Roku Channel and LG Channels). Third-party apps like Netflix and YouTube? No ACR except a small amount on webOS, which disappears when opted out. Screen mirroring also looks to be safe from monitoring on all TVs but the one running Vidaa OS. To figure out whether each OS used audio or video fingerprinting, the experimenters played content that had both video and audio, just audio with a black screen, and just video with no audio, and watched for changes in network traffic to the ACR endpoints. They found that Tizen likely uses video fingerprinting, webOS and Vidaa use audio, and Fire TV OS, Google TV OS, Roku OS, and Vizio OS use a combination of both. Ideally, opting out of ACR activity should stop all data transmission to suspected ACR endpoints, and for webOS, Fire OS, Vidaa OS, and the Sony Google TV, that’s what happened. But it wasn’t always the case. Samsung’s Tizen OS activity decreased, but not completely, with ACR-correlated traffic still showing while using the antenna, first-party streaming, and HDMI. And on the two Roku OS TVs (one from TCL and one from Roku), ACR still applied to the Roku Channel app. TCL discloses this limitation in menu settings, while the Roku TV does not. Opting out on the Vizio TV didn’t change ACR-correlated traffic at all. (Vizio settled a lawsuit with the FTC in 2017 related to consumer data gathering.) I reached out to Walmart for comment about the Vizio TV’s performance in the study but did not hear back before press time. As the paper notes, because almost all network traffic sent from the TVs to the suspected ACR endpoints was encrypted, the researchers couldn’t be entirely sure that the traffic that remained after opting out was ACR traffic. “We interpret the continued presence of traffic consistent with ACR tracking after opt-out as suspicious, though we cannot confirm the contents of the network traffic (due to encryption), nor whether data is processed or retained on the server side.” It doesn’t seem to matter if you opt out during the setup process or later down the line. “For the large-scale automated tests, we applied the opt-out through the TVs’ settings menus after setup, not during the setup process,” project lead professor David Choffnes told The Verge via email. But the researchers “also manually tested certain TVs (the Vizio TV and the Fire TV) after a factory reset, and the results were unchanged,” he told me. The testing order was also randomized to prevent earlier experiments from influencing later ones. [Image: TVs primarily track data over the antenna, HDMI, and with first-party streaming services such as The Roku Channel on a Roku TV. Disturbingly, during the study, the researchers discovered a vulnerability with Vidaa OS exposing unencrypted information. Because of the vulnerability, the researchers were able to access an MQTT broker — an intermediary between Vidaa OS and Unruly, a video ad platform — and receive ACR results from other Vidaa TV users. > “Each message carries a Client ID, a permanent identifier for the TV that can’t be reset, along with the time zone, the app name, the input (antenna, HDMI), the antenna channel and an audio fingerprint.” Over a period of three hours, they collected data from over 1 million unique TVs. They informed Vidaa of the vulnerability, which the company confirmed and has since addressed by requiring a login for the server (although messages are still sent unencrypted). [Image: After opting out of ACR, tracking stopped on most TVs, but some traffic was still detected with Tizen OS, Roku OS, and especially Vizio OS. The paper recommends ways to protect ourselves from TVs harvesting our data. The easiest is to disconnect your TV from the internet, both wired and wireless, and instead use a streaming device that doesn’t run ACR. If you want to continue using the built-in apps, they suggest using webOS, Fire TV OS, Google TV on Sony, and Vidaa OS — just make sure to opt out of everything you can. They also provide a blocklist of endpoints you can restrict using blockers like Pi-hole that don’t break the TVs or affect view quality. The researchers call on TV makers to make changes, including listing every input that ACR watches and putting that information in the privacy policy (some companies do this more clearly than others), and to authenticate and encrypt all ACR traffic. And they say regulators need to hold manufacturers to task and make sure opt-out agreements work fully to protect us. I agree that there needs to be more transparency from TV manufacturers about ACR and, more broadly, what data of ours they collect and when. The Northeastern study helps to pinpoint when data is gathered, but there’s still a lot that’s seemingly intentionally hidden. And it shouldn’t be up to independent researchers to discover and disclose any of this. It should be the responsibility of the companies doing the collecting. It’s time for them to stop hiding what they’re doing.

articles.title: Bluetooth is getting a big boost to data transfer speeds
articles.summary: The Bluetooth SIG has officially adopted a new feature called High Data Throughput that increases the speed and bandwidth of the popular wireless format.
articles.body: The Bluetooth Special Interest Group (SIG) that oversees the wireless standard has formally adopted Bluetooth High Data Throughput (HDT) as an optional feature of the Bluetooth Core 7.0. It’s an upgrade the Bluetooth SIG has been previewing over the past year that increases Bluetooth LE’s maximum supported bit rate from 2 Mbps to 7.5 Mbps. It will allow for higher resolution audio to be streamed but also improvements to battery life and reliability. The primary application for Bluetooth HDT will once again be for wireless audio, with the first devices supporting the new feature expected to appear sometime in 2027. The increased bit rate will support high-resolution audio but also new wireless audio experiences including spatial audio and multi-channel surround sound without requiring proprietary wireless formats. [Image: The Bluetooth SIG has been demonstrating the Bluetooth HDT upgrades over the past year. Bluetooth HDT will benefit other wireless devices beyond headphones. Smartwatches could sync more training, health, and fitness data to a phone without a reduction in battery life because HDT can transfer more data in less time, requiring the Bluetooth radio to be on for shorter periods. Spatial computing and extended reality devices could offer more robust experiences without needing a connection to Wi-Fi, and HDT will benefit the ever-growing number of personal AI devices, allowing them to more efficiently hand off data to be processed by a smartphone so they can be lighter and smaller. Even the simple act of updating the firmware on a smartwatch or smart home accessories could feel faster and become a task that doesn’t need to be put off until later when you’re not using your device. “Bluetooth HDT brings a new level of performance to Bluetooth technology, expanding the role it can play across consumer, commercial, and industrial markets and creating a powerful foundation for the next generation of wireless innovation,” said Neville Meijers, CEO of the Bluetooth SIG. “As the world’s most widely used wireless standard, Bluetooth technology has continually evolved to meet the growing demands of an increasingly connected world.”

articles.title: Stunt Coordinator Geeta Tandon calls out disrespect on Anil Kapoor's show India Ke Top 1%; Actor reacts to her allegations
articles.summary: Stunt coordinator Geeta Tandon has accused the team of Anil Kapoor's show India Ke Top 1% of disrespect.
articles.body: Stunt coordinator Geeta Tandon has accused the team of Anil Kapoor's show India Ke Top 1% of disrespect. She claimed that she and her son were invited as guests for an upcoming episode but waited for nine hours, with no clear update from the production team. 3. She also alleged that the production manager was dismissive when she asked why they were being made to wait.Geeta took to her social media account to share an eight-slide post in which she mentioned about being invited as a guest on the show along with her son. She further said that she joined the show without payment for exposure but felt disrespected by how things were handled.The former Khatron Ke Khiladi contestant revealed she and her son arrived on the set at 12:30 pm. They were then informed that the segment would be shot in a few hours. According to Geeta, they waited for almost nine hours without being informed about the delay. They were made to wait inside a tent with no proper explanation from the production team.She also revealed that she kept asking the non-fiction show's team for updates but was not given any proper information. "I gave up a day's work and even called my son back from Goa specifically for the shoot," she wrote.Geeta shared that she confronted the team over the long wait and their behaviour. She wrote in her post that the production manager, Jaydeep, responded, "If they want to leave, let them leave. But they can't leave without signing."This did not go well with Geeta, who asked the show's team why she and her son were not allowed to leave without signing a document. Geeta said she refused to accept their behaviour and added that they left the set at 9:15 pm after waiting for nearly nine hours."I did not come there asking for a favour. Your team invited me. Your team repeatedly followed up with me. I gave you my time, my professional commitments and my son's time, without asking for a single rupee. The least I expected was basic human dignity," she wrote.She tagged the production house, host Anil Kapoor and special guest for the episode Farah Khan, informing them about the mismanagement. However, she set the record straight that she doesn't blame the actor or the filmmaker for personally instructing the team to treat her that way. She just wanted to inform them about her experience on the sets.She said, "Being a celebrity should not determine how much respect someone deserves. The person standing behind the camera deserves the same dignity as the person standing in front of it."Farah Khan and Anil Kapoor respond to Geeta's postFarah Khan replied to Geeta's post and apologised for the incident. She said she was unaware that Geeta was waiting on the set, as she was busy shooting the second episode in the evening. Farah commented on her post, "Geetaji apologies.. I had no idea you were there as I was shooting for the 2nd episode in the evening.. otherwise would have made you sit in my van. As would Anil if he knew.. we have tremendous respect for you and your hard work."Anil Kapoor also reacted to the stunt coordinator's post. He said he was sorry to hear about her experience and the way she and her son were treated. "Geeta ji, it genuinely saddens me to hear this. As the host, I always wanted everyone who was part of the show to feel welcome and respected. You and your son came as our guests. I'm sorry that your experience left you feeling otherwise," he wrote.Anil Kapoor also mentioned in the comment that her feedback mattered to him and that respect should be given to everyone in the industry. Geeta thanked the actor for his response and hoped others would not face the same situation.Get the latest TV News, TV Shows and more. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Rian Johnson explains why he had to build his own iPhone camera app
articles.summary: Chromagraph Camera lets anyone with an iPhone get the look used by the director of Knives Out and The Last Jedi.
articles.body: Rian Johnson is an analog photography devotee. The director of Knives Out and The Last Jedi can often be spotted on set with a Leica M6 at his side, documenting production on film. But sometimes, it’s still easier to reach for a phone. So Johnson started wondering if the photos from his iPhone could be made to look more like the grade he applies to his movies. The result is Chromagraph Camera, a $13 iOS app that bypasses elements of Apple’s image processing pipeline and applies the same look used on Johnson’s movies. The app, made by Johnson and his longtime cinematographer, Steve Yedlin, is shockingly simple, with just a few primary settings, but it gives anyone who buys it access to image processing decisions good enough for a Hollywood production. “The reality is, as much as I love my Leica, as much as I love my other gear, it’s a pain in the butt having a camera on your shoulder, or a massive backpack with four cameras in it,” Johnson says. “And I always have my phone with me.” [Media: Watch | Listen | Get ad-free Johnson has been tinkering with phone photography for a long time. Back before the smartphone days, he bought a Nokia phone with a proper camera — at least, proper for the time. “It was like the first one where they advertised the camera on it as the main feature of it,” he says. “And it was garbage, the camera was awful, but it took these photos that were grainy and contrasty and funky and beautiful.” Smartphone photography has progressed substantially since then, but that progression has also come with a loss of character. The default photos coming out of modern phones tend to look sharper, brighter, and more clinical than in the days before computational photography took hold. You can work around this, but it generally means shooting RAW and editing the images yourself. [Image: [Image: Initially, Johnson tried shooting with the iPhone’s default camera and editing in Snapseed to get his desired look. He then graduated to third-party RAW camera apps, only to get bogged down shuffling files back and forth and tweaking endless sliders. “I would do a lot of messing with every photo,” he says, “and then it was a little like I’d wandered through the woods and I wasn’t sure how I’d gotten there.” Smartphone makers have started including tools to add more character to their images. Apple added a texture panel with film, grain, and halation settings to the iPhone 18 Pro, and Google put a new “Camera Looks” panel in the Pixel 11. But these still don’t afford the level of control you get from starting with a RAW image. And if you really want to dial in a look that feels unique to you, that’s what you need to start with. Yedlin is convinced that given the right set of algorithms and settings, there is no perceivable difference between an image shot on film and one shot on digital. A few years back, he set out to make a series of color grading scripts to give Johnson’s movies the organic look of celluloid. Eventually, those tools allowed Johnson to apply their movie color pipeline to his still RAW files and film scans. That gave Johnson the confidence to bring the same ideas to mobile. [Image: [Image: “I knew he could do it,” Johnson says. “I called Steve up and bullied him ... I kept saying, ‘Can we do it for iPhone photos?’” Chromagraph Camera is a camera, of course, with settings for maximum exposure time, burst mode, and color tuning, but maybe one of the most fun things to do is to import RAW images you’ve already shot and process them in the app. It’s a camera and editor in one, but I’ve found myself importing old RAWs and seeing what Yedlin’s film-like processing does to my existing library. It doesn’t work for every photo right out of the gate, but after import you’ll have tons of options for tuning, like tone, color, saturation, and texture. [Image: [Image: Johnson’s app is clearly still in its early stages, with settings and UI elements laid out in sometimes unexpected places. But the core of the app, the processing, is what is drawing people toward it. Over the weekend, Chromagraph went viral on social media, with many early users marveling at the app’s results compared to Apple’s defaults. Even though this app gives Johnson what he’s been craving with smartphone photography, he remains entranced by much earlier photographic techniques. While chatting with me over coffee, I saw his eyes light up when he started talking about the 8 x 10 wet plate photography he’s been experimenting with at home. He even recently set up his own darkroom and continues to experiment with the chaotic, exciting art of analog photography. “It’s like nerd fishing,” he says. “It’s about the actual process of doing it for me.” Photography by David Imel / The Verge
